findings.title: Cleanup routine logs normal operation at Error level, including full ID lists
findings.body: The new cleanup code logs every batch at Error level: `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...)` (line 534), `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", ...)` (line 537), and the equivalents for count-based cleanup (lines 554, 557) and orphaned tag cleanup (lines 576, 579). These are not errors — they fire on every successful batch of a job that runs on a schedule, and they include the full `ids` slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries per line). This will flood error-level logs, trigger log-based alerting on errors that aren't errors, and produce very large log lines. They should be Debug level.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all cleanup jobs
findings.body: This PR changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This does not just make annotation cleanup run more often — it makes every cleanup job (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, temp user invites, short URLs, query history, tmp file deletion) run 10x more frequently. Several of these do non-trivial database deletes and filesystem scans, and query history cleanup enforces row limits over large tables. This is an undocumented, broad behavioral/performance change bundled into a PR about avoiding annotation deadlocks; if the intent was only to make annotation cleanup more responsive, the annotation job should get its own schedule rather than speeding up the entire cleanup loop.

findings.title: MaxCount cleanup can exit early if a fetched batch is concurrently deleted
findings.body: In the new split fetch-then-delete flow, `untilDoneOrCancelled` stops when a batch reports zero affected rows. Because the SELECT and DELETE are no longer in one statement/transaction, another process (e.g., a second Grafana instance's cleanup job, or a user delete) can delete the fetched IDs between the two statements, making `RowsAffected()` return 0 and terminating the loop even though more annotations beyond MaxCount still exist. The old single-statement form re-evaluated the subquery on each execution and only stopped when a delete genuinely matched nothing. The under-deleted rows will be cleaned on the next cycle so the impact is bounded, but it is a behavioral regression worth noting/acknowledging (e.g., loop while len(ids) == batchSize instead of affected > 0).
